activities.caption: drag between the two ways of knowing
activities.name: anArmchairCompare

config.prompt: Two methods, separated by an ocean. Drag the divider.

before.label: armchair synthesis (before 1914)
before.text: Scholars synthesised reports from traders, missionaries and colonial officers, separated from their data by oceans. Nothing could surface that no one had thought to report — the Kula ring was invisible to this method.

after.label: fieldwork (Malinowski's standard)
after.text: Live in the midst of the people studied, learn the language, participate in daily life, and record the 'imponderabilia of actual life' — the routines no one thinks to tell an outsider because no one thinks of them at all.

config.why: Its two lessons still define the craft: immersion is not decoration but evidence (meaning lives in context), and the ethnographer's body in the field is the instrument — which makes calibrating the instrument a methodological problem in itself.

activities.anchor: written daily, ideally in two registers
activities.caption: file each entry into its register
activities.name: anFieldnoteBuckets

config.prompt: Fieldnotes are written daily in two registers, kept separate so observation and interpretation do not contaminate each other at the source. File each entry:

items.label: who sat where, who spoke first, who left
a hunch that the harvest ritual tracks the debt cycle
a question to test next week about gift reciprocity

config.why: The split is methodological, not stylistic: mixing them at the source makes the inference from observation to claim unauditable.

activities.anchor: The conventional duration of a year or more
activities.caption: pair each fieldcraft choice with its reason
activities.name: anFieldcraftMatch

config.prompt: Each working practice has a rationale. Match them:

pairs.left: a year or more in the field
pairs.right: captures a full annual cycle — and outlasts the initial performance of the guest role
every key informant is a perspective, not a window
who brokers access shapes what you can see
keeps observation and interpretation from contaminating each other

config.why: After the guest-role performance wears off, ordinary unrehearsed life becomes observable — which is why the duration is not ritual.

activities.anchor: the insider's (emic) account is the true one
activities.caption: true or false — emic, etic and the twitch
activities.name: anEmicJudge

statements.s: The insider's (emic) account is the true one and the analyst's (etic) account a distortion.
statements.why: They answer different questions. Participants cannot report their own taken-for-granted world any more than a fish can report water.

statements.s: The difference between a twitch and a wink is semiotic, not muscular.
statements.why: Only context separates them, and ethnography's object is exactly that difference.

statements.s: Ethnography is just hanging out and writing it up.
statements.why: The immersion is instrumented: structured observation, interview schedules, life histories, genealogies, mapping, surveys — all triangulated.

statements.s: Coding and negative-case analysis are the qualitative analogue of falsification.
statements.why: Hunting what breaks your emerging account is the discipline's version of trying to disprove yourself.

activities.caption: bet on what the critique changed
activities.name: anWritingCulturePredict

config.q: What did the Writing Culture critique (1986) argue about ethnographic texts?
choices: That ethnography should abandon writing and use film instead
That a text in one voice, with one authority, silently manufactures an omniscience the field never had
That ethnographers should stop studying other cultures
That fieldnotes should be published verbatim instead of analysed
config.why: Ethnographic authority was constructed — the all-seeing fieldworker voice erased dialogue and position. The response (polyphony, dialogic editing, participant co-authorship) changed practice, unevenly.

activities.anchor: the observer effect at human scale
activities.caption: fill the honest standard
activities.name: anReflexivityCloze

config.text: Since the ethnographer is the instrument, the instrument's properties must be reported: that is %%0%%. The honest standard is not neutrality but %%1%% — no one escapes a standpoint, so the accountable researcher maps theirs and shows their work.
config.hint: The first names the practice of documenting how your position shaped what you could see; the second is the standard it buys, contrasted with neutrality.

activities.anchor: signed consent forms make fieldwork ethical
activities.caption: decide the hard ethics case
activities.name: anEthicsBranch

config.root: You have consent forms signed by every participant. Then a court subpoenas your fieldnotes, and a participant faces consequences for what they told you.

start.text: The form is signed and the research was approved. What does the modern standard require now?

choices.label: Hand over the notes — the consent form covers the research
choices.feedback: Fieldnotes have been subpoenaed and seized; the encrypted-notes standard exists precisely because this happens.

choices.label: Treat consent as a continuing relationship, not a signature
choices.feedback: Consent in forms communities can actually exercise, plus reciprocity and data sovereignty.

handover.text: The participants bear the cost of a signature they could not have understood as a subpoena waiver.

relationship.text: Research with, not on: the small-population identifiability problem, the seizure problem and the refusal problem are exactly the ones forms cannot carry.

config.why: The Yanomami controversy permanently changed governance: pre-fieldwork review, informed consent in forms communities can actually exercise, reciprocity, data sovereignty, and the right of communities to review or refuse research about them.

activities.anchor: the second answer, after the pause, is often the real
activities.caption: order the interviewing craft, weakest to strongest
activities.name: anInterviewOrder

config.prompt: The lesson ranks interview craft moves. Put them from the most basic to the most diagnostic:
items: Ask open questions before closed ones
Use silence as a tool — the second answer after the pause is often the real one
Chase examples: 'tell me about the last time' beats 'do you usually'
Triangulate against observation — where talk and practice diverge is where the findings live
config.why: Interviews are performances mutually staged: what a person tells a known outsider is a social fact about the relationship, not a window onto private truth.

activities.caption: rank reciprocity by social distance
activities.name: anReciprocityOrder

config.prompt: Sahlins systematised the logic: reciprocity shades with social distance. Order from closest to coldest:
items: Generalised — give without accounting, as among kin
Balanced — even, timed exchange, as between trade partners
Negative — get the better, as in market haggling at its coldest
config.why: What you may expect back IS who someone is to you — exchange is a social map continuously redrawn.

activities.caption: find the faulty line in this gift argument
activities.name: anGiftSpot

config.prompt: A student writes up Mauss. One line is wrong — find it.
lines: Mauss found no 'pure' gifts: giving, receiving and reciprocating are all obligatory.
A gift creates no obligation — what is freely given is free, and that freedom is the point.
The obligation is the point: gifts weave total social systems, binding giver and receiver across time.
The potlatch was misread as irrational waste — Canada banned it in the 1880s — when it was a status-and-obligation system.
Kula valuables circulate for decades instead of being consumed: the object is the relationship's bookmark.
config.correction: A gift does create obligation — giving, receiving and reciprocating are all compulsory moves, and the apparent freedom is the disguise.
config.why: The convergence is striking: behavioural economics' ultimatum-game refusals of 'unfair' offers look, from this side, like Mauss's obligated reciprocators — two traditions arriving at the same human from opposite directions.

activities.caption: drag between two economic orders
activities.name: anEmbeddedCompare

config.prompt: Polanyi's historical frame. Drag the divider.

before.label: embedded economies
before.text: Production and distribution organised by kinship, reciprocity, redistribution from temple and chiefly storage, and householding. The economy is a function of social relations.

after.label: the self-regulating market
after.text: Land, labour and money treated as commodities, with prices clearing without social permission. A recent, deliberately institutionalised design — and a fragile one, which is what Polanyi's double movement describes.

config.why: The productive residue of the substantivist-formalist debate: allocate formal analysis where it fits — the rational peasant is a real finding — while insisting that prices, property and even 'profit' are institutionally constituted.

activities.caption: file each transaction into its Tiv sphere
activities.name: anTivBuckets

config.prompt: Bohannan's Tiv sorted transactions into ranked, morally bounded categories. File each:
config.why: Conversion between spheres was fraught, and colonial currency's arrival collapsed the boundaries in a generation, with moral chaos following.

activities.caption: true or false — what money may not buy
activities.name: anBlockedJudge

statements.s: Money is culturally neutral — cash is cash, and whatever it touches becomes equivalent.
statements.why: Every society fences categories its currency may not buy: votes, honours, human beings, blood, sexual access, kidneys.

statements.s: Paid US blood systems produced better supply and safety than voluntary donation.
statements.why: Titmuss found the reverse — the market crowding out the gift made supply worse and less safe.

statements.s: Which things are commodifiable is a society's ongoing moral settlement.
statements.why: Redesigning money redesigns the settlement — the anthropological point is anti-universalist, not anti-market.

statements.s: Colonial currency collapsed the Tiv's spheres within a generation.
statements.why: Centuries of moral boundaries undone by a new medium.

activities.caption: pair each political form with its organising principle
activities.name: anPolityMatch

config.prompt: Service's sequence orders the comparative record. Match each form to how it runs:

pairs.right: egalitarian foragers, leadership by achievement, conflict managed by mobility and fission
segmentary lineages and age-sets, the 'big man' who must re-earn position by giving
hereditary hierarchy, redistribution from stored surplus, monumental labour
centralised monopoly of legitimate force, law, bureaucracy

config.why: The chiefdom's defining feature — redistribution and ascribed rank — is precisely what big-man systems lack: the big man must re-earn position continuously; the chief inherits it.

activities.caption: file each form of resistance by how it reads to power
activities.name: anResistanceBuckets

config.prompt: Where open rebellion is suicidal, the dominated resist everyday and deniably. File each:

items.label: a manifesto and a general strike

config.why: Everyday forms leave no manifesto and, precisely for that reason, elude state archives — which is why they were invisible to political science until Scott looked.

activities.caption: bet on who controls the money
activities.name: anHouseholdPredict

config.q: The household is often modelled as a single unit with pooled interests. What does the intra-household allocation literature find instead?
choices: Pooling is accurate — who receives income makes no measurable difference
Resources behave differently depending on who controls them, with women's income shifting spending toward children's food, health and schooling
Men systematically spend more on children than women do
The effect exists but is too small to change policy design
config.why: It demolished the unitary model and changed development policy instrument by instrument — cash transfers to mothers, microcredit focused on women's groups.

activities.caption: guess the reach of one man's line
activities.name: anStarClusterEstimate

config.prompt: A Y-chromosome lineage appears in roughly 8% of men across the former Mongol empire. About how many living male descendants is that?
config.why: Around 16 million living male descendants of one man who lived about a millennium ago, plausibly Genghis Khan's male line. A single person's reproductive reach can reshape a continent's gene pool.
config.context: Sixteen million men — the agency lens at continental scale.

activities.anchor: The Durkheimian lens asks what held people together
activities.caption: reverse the ritual-first sequence
activities.name: anRitualFirstOrder

config.prompt: The cohesion lens predicts that the biggest Neolithic architecture is ritual architecture. Order the Göbekli Tepe argument:
items: Carved megalithic enclosures stand from about 9600 BCE
They were built by foragers, before farming in the region
So collective ceremony was not a luxury agriculture paid for
Ritual may have been the coordination technology that drew people into settlement, with farming following the feast
config.why: Cohesion reads palaeolithic cave art the same way: costly, coordinated, culturally rehearsed activity creating the shared symbols and mutual obligations that make large groups possible.

activities.caption: bet on what the cemetery shows
activities.name: anJebelSahabaPredict

config.q: Jebel Sahaba (Sudan, about 13,000 years ago) preserves skeletons with embedded projectile points and both healed and unhealed wounds. What does the pattern suggest?
choices: A single massacre in one afternoon
Repeated raids over time, not one event
Ritual burial practice with no violence
config.why: Healed wounds alongside unhealed ones mean people survived some attacks and died in others — repeated raids. It is one of the earliest known cemeteries of interpersonal violence.

activities.caption: file each lens by the question it asks
activities.name: anLensBuckets

config.prompt: The chapter runs several lenses over the same record. File each lens by the question it asks:
buckets: What kind of cause it was

items.label: diachronic — sequences dated by multiple clocks
agency — identifiable actors and innovation capture
idealist — causes in ideas and symbols

config.why: The diachronic lens is deep history's default: it studies sequences, and its discipline is checking the clocks against each other, since each error the others catch.

activities.caption: combine the lenses on one replacement
activities.name: anReplacementBranch

config.root: Ancient DNA shows about 90% ancestry replacement in Britain around 4,400 years ago.

start.text: How do you interpret a replacement that large?

choices.label: Conflict lens alone: it must have been a slaughter
choices.feedback: Differential reproduction can take over a gene pool quietly — the record does not require mass killing.

choices.label: Combine lenses: migration plus differential reproduction, with conflict as one possible component
choices.feedback: The conflict lens explains replacement events without requiring slaughter.

slaughter.text: You have read a demographic process as a single event, and the archaeology of violence does not show the massacre you need.

combined.text: Migration, advantage and reproduction together can replace 90% of a gene pool across generations — which is why the lenses are lenses and not a single verdict.

config.why: The conflict lens has its own material record — embedded points, healed fractures, burial wealth differences marking hereditary status — but it explains replacement without requiring slaughter.

activities.anchor: farming independently invented in at least three regions
activities.caption: fill the master sequence
activities.name: anSequenceCloze

config.text: The master sequence: anatomically modern humans in Africa by about %%0%% years ago; the main expansion out of Africa around 70,000–50,000 years ago; the Americas by about 20,000–15,000 years ago; farming independently invented in at least %%1%% regions between about 11,000 and 7,000 years ago.
config.hint: The African date is the Jebel Irhoud figure; the farming inventions numbered at least this many regions.

activities.caption: date the oldest known figurative art
activities.name: anSulawesiPlace

config.prompt: The Sulawesi pig painting is the oldest known figurative art. Place the marker at its date, in thousands of years ago.
config.why: About 45,500 years ago — part of the marked flowering of figurative art, ornament, notation and ritual burial from roughly 50,000–40,000 years ago.

activities.caption: pair each lens with its deep-history case
activities.name: anLensCaseMatch

config.prompt: Each lens found real structure. Match lens to its exemplar:

pairs.right: the star cluster in the Mongol empire's gene pool
Göbekli Tepe's ritual enclosures built before farming
burial wealth differences and children buried with goods they could not have earned
the symbolic revolution in art, ornament and ritual burial

config.why: Inequality has its own archaeology: lavish goods buried with children mark hereditary status appearing with farming and storage, roughly 10,000 years ago — the deep origin of the class question.
